- e) The Petitioner kept SECI informed of the aforesaid circumstances throughout. The Respondent has acknowledged the problems faced by the Petitioner and has made efforts to assist the Petitioner in securing the said land-related approvals for the Project.

- a) The Petitioner is raising the issues of Force Majeure as a cover-up to wriggle out of the committed agreement resulting from the selection of and issue of the Letter of Award to the Petitioner for establishing the 200 MW Wind Power Project for the generation and supply of electricity to enable SECI to resell the same to UPPCL under the PSA. The signing of the PPA post-issuance of the Letter of Award was the sole responsibility of the Petitioner (Clause 3.32 of the RfS).

- a) The Petitioner’s contention is that, as the PPA was not executed by the Petitioner as per the draft, forming part of the bid documents, there is no existing, concluded or binding

- b) On the basis of the above development, a binding and enforceable agreement came into existence as per the draft terms and conditions of the PPA circulated in the bidding process, and the Petitioner, having accepted the terms and conditions while submitting its bid, notwithstanding the refusal of the Petitioner to sign the PPA.  In the facts and circumstances of the present case, the signing of the PPA is a ministerial act and not a condition precedent  to the effectiveness of the agreement which has resulted from the bidding process.

- f) The Petitioner cannot claim the alleged force majeure affecting the implementation of the project as a ground for not signing the PPA. In terms of the RfS and the LoA, the PPA was required within three months (90 days) from the LoA. There was no force majeure event that impacted the signing of the PPA. The issue of an alleged force majeure event affecting the implementation of the PPA, even if, for the sake of argument, it  were accepted, could have been raised only after the signing of the PPA.

13. From the submissions of the contracting parties, the following issues emerge for adjudication before the Commission:

_implementation of the Project; delay in tariff adoption and approval of Power Sale Agreement by the Regulatory Commissions._ The Petitioner is accordingly seeking discharge from the obligations/liabilities, including the execution of the PPA and establishment of the project, towards the Respondents. _Per Contra,_ Respondents SECI and UPPCL submitted that the responsibility for the selection, identification, procurement, or leasing of land, and for obtaining clear possession of 100% of the land, falls within the scope of responsibility of the Petitioner and is to be exclusively undertaken by the Petitioner at its own cost and risk. Hence, the arrangement of land for setting up the project cannot be claimed as a ground for delay in signing the PPA. The inability of the contractors hired by the Petitioner is a matter exclusively between the Petitioner and its contractors and cannot be pleaded as a ground for failing to execute the PPA. Further, SECI has submitted that since the Petitioner has refused to sign the PPA with SECI within the stipulated time period, i.e. by 23.11.2021 (final time granted by SECI for signing of PPA), SECI is entitled to encash the Bank Guarantee equivalent to the amount of Earnest Money Deposit, i.e. 12,00,00,000 and the project of the Petitioner stands cancelled. UPPCL has submitted that on account of non-signing of the PPA by the Petitioner, even after being issued the LoA and after identification of such power for resale to UPPCL, constitutes a breach on the part of the Petitioner, and as such, UPPCL has suffered a legal injury on account of the refusal of the Petitioner to sign the PPA.

23. We note that as per the provisions of the RfS dated 22.02.2019, MoP guidelines dated 08.12.2017 and the Standard PPA, it was the duty of the Petitioner for selection/identification/procurement of land, getting clear possession of 100% of the land, etc. Moreover, the Petitioner was free to choose any land for implementing the project. There was no compulsion to construct the project only on the revenue land, and the Petitioner could have explored other opportunities. We also note that the financial inability of the Petitioner’s contractors cannot be the ground for non-commissioning of the project, as the inability of the contractors/agents appointed by the Petitioner to undertake the tasks is a matter entirely

## **ORDER** 

The Petitioner, Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (‘CTUIL’), has filed the present Petition seeking necessary directions and/or guidelines in regard to the nature and treatment of extensions by Renewable Energy Implementation Agencies (REIAs) or distribution licensees for the purposes of compliance with Regulation 11A and Regulation 24 of the GNA Regulations, 2022. 

2. The Petitioner has filed the present Petition seeking the following relief(s): 

_(a) Exercise its powers under Regulation 42 (Power to Remove Difficulties) of the GNA Regulations, 2022 to issue such directions or guidelines as may be necessary in regard to nature and treatment of the extensions by REIAs or Distribution Licensees for the purposes of compliance of Regulation 11A and Regulation 24 of the GNA Regulations, 2022;_ 

_(b) Issue directions/ clarification in regard to the extension granted to Azure by SECI and consequent exclusion of Azure from the Revocation List; and_ 

_(c) Pass such further order(s) or direction(s) as this Commission may deem just and proper in the facts and circumstances of the present case._ 

3. The matter was heard on 3.6.2026. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the present Petition has been filed seeking necessary directions and/or guidelines in regard to the nature and treatment of extensions by Renewable Energy Implementation Agencies (REIAs) or distribution licensees for the purposes of compliance with Regulation 11A and Regulation 24 of the GNA Regulations. The learned counsel, while pointing out one such extension granted by 

Order in Petition No. 259/MP/2026 

**2** 

SECI in the case of the Respondent No.1/APIPL, submitted that APIPL was granted Connectivity(ies) with a specified commissioning timeline of 30.9.2021, and the last date for compliance with Regulation 24.6 of GNA Regulations worked out as 31.12.2025. However, SECI _vide_ letter dated 9.1.2026 communicated the revised/ extended SCD for the awarded project capacity for which the PPAs were yet to be signed and requested that they be considered an extension of the SCD for the purposes of Regulation 24.6. However, in respect of 250 MW of awarded capacity, for which the SCD had been revised to 31.3.2028, a condition was imposed stating that the SCD considered the PSA/PPA signing by 31.3.2026. Based on the said letter from SECI, the Petitioner, as a matter of prudence, excluded APIPL’s name from the revocation list published on its portal on 20.1.2026 pertaining to non-compliance under Regulation 24.6 of GNA Regulations. However, since the extended SCD of 250 MW was stated to be contingent upon the signing of the PPA/PSA by 31.3.2026, CTUIL expressly reserved its right to seek necessary clarification or direction from the appropriate regulatory, adjudicatory or jurisdictional authority. The learned counsel further submitted that, as per CTUIL’s information, no PPA/PSA was signed by 31.3.2026, and CTUIL, therefore, on 1.6.2026, proceeded to revoke APIPL’s 250 MW Connectivity(ies)/deemed GNA and invoked the Connectivity Bank Guarantees furnished by it. The learned counsel also pointed out that subsequent to the filing  of the present Petition, the Commission, in its recent order dated 31.5.2026 in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 (Datta Power Infra Private Limited v CTUIL), has already clarified that the tentative SCOD, based on the tentative PPA that is yet to be signed, is not a valid document for the extension of SCOD, and thus, the issue raised in the present case stands addressed in terms thereof. 

4. The matter was mentioned by the learned counsel for the Petitioner on 11.6.2026 and apprised that the Respondent, APIPL, is pursuing a separate Petition 

Order in Petition No. 259/MP/2026 

**3** 

(Diary) No. 388/2026 along with IA (Diary) No. 389/2026, seeking quashing of the revocation of APIPL’s connectivity and other reliefs. Therefore, in terms of the order dated 31.5.2026 in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 (Datta Power Infra Private Limited v CTUIL), nothing survives in the instant Petition. The learned counsel for the Petitioner sought permission to withdraw the instant Petition. The learned counsel for the Respondent, APIPL, did not oppose the Petitioner’s request for withdrawal of the Petition. 

5.     Considering the submissions of the learned counsels for the parties, the Petitioner is permitted to withdraw the present Petition. 

6. Petition No. 259/MP/2026 is disposed of as withdrawn.

The present Petition is filed by the Petitioner, M.P. Power Management Company Ltd. (MPMCL), for seeking payment of the balance outstanding amount of Rs 83.229 crore by the Respondent, UP Power Corporation Ltd (UPPCL), along with interest (in compliance with the decision in MoM dated 9.8.2018) pertaining to Rihand and Matatila Hydro Power Station.

## **Background** 

2. Rihand (300 MW) and Matatila (30 MW) Hydel Stations were commissioned in 1966 and 1965, respectively. As per the agreement dated 09.01.1963, UP was required to supply 15% of the power from Rihand and a one-third share from Matatila to MP due to the submergence of land in MP. Since disputes arose regarding nonsupply of power and compensation, MP filed Petition No. 107/2007 before the Commission. The Commission, vide order dated 12.11.2008, directed UPPCL to pay compensation to MP, which was upheld by APTEL vide judgment dated 21.07.2011 in Appeal No. 151/2008. Subsequently, disputes regarding Rajghat HPS and compensation were also adjudicated by the Commission. Thereafter, APTEL, in Appeal Nos. 59/2014 and 120/2014, directed both States to explore amicable settlement of disputes. Pursuant thereto, and in compliance with the decision recorded in the MoM dated 09.08.2018, a settlement was arrived at whereby UPPCL was required to pay Rs. 157.782 crore to MPPMCL in instalments. However, UPPCL paid only Rs. 74.553 crore, leaving a balance amount of Rs. 83.229 crore unpaid, which led to the present dispute. 

3. The Petition was admitted on 13.04.2023, Subsequently, the matter was listed for hearing on 10.08.2023, 10.10.2023, 21.2.2024, 02.07.2025, 12.08.2025, 26.09.2025, 27.11.2025, and 18.03.2026. During the hearing on 10.10.2023, the Commission directed the parties to explore the possibility of a mutual settlement of the issues. 

4. The Petitioner vide affidavit dated 15.5.2026, and the respondent vide affidavit dated 14.5.2026, have submitted that the issues involved in the present petition have been mutually settled between the parties and have requested that the present petition be dismissed as withdrawn.

8. The matter was listed for hearing on 15.1.2026 and 3.3.2026. During the hearing on 3.3.2026, the learned counsel for the Petitioner, while reiterating the submissions made in the Petition, submitted that, in compliance with the Record of Proceedings dated 16.12.2025, the Petitioner has also filed its note of submissions dated 2.3.2026, indicating the reasons for seeking the period of three years to reduce its shareholding to 5%.

10. In response, the learned counsel for the Petitioner strongly opposed the prayer of IEX for the impleadment and submitted that the matter being regulatory in nature did not need the intervention of a third party. The learned counsel also submitted that IEX had no locus standi in this case as it was not in any way an aggrieved person.

11. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties, the Commission reserved the Petition as well as IA for order.

12. We have considered the submissions by the Petitioner and the Intervenor, IEX. The present Petition has been filed by the Petitioner seeking the grant of time to one of the promoter shareholders, namely PTC, to dilute its stake in the Petitioner Company to meet the requirements/ compliance under Regulation 15 of the PMR 2021. However, before dealing with the above aspect, it is necessary to first decide on the application filed by IEX, seeking impleadment as a party Respondent in the present Petition and permission to file its reply.

without any application, and on such terms as may appear to it to be just, direct that any of the following persons may be added as a party: (a) any person who ought to have been joined as plaintiff or defendant, but not added; or (b) any person whose presence before the court may be necessary in order to enable the court to effectively and completely adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit. This Commission is vested with a similar discretion by virtue of Regulation 37 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission ( _Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023_ . However, it is equally trite law that if a person is not found to be “a proper party” or “a necessary party”, the court does not have jurisdiction to order his impleadment against the wishes of a Plaintiff. A “necessary party” is a person who ought to have been joined as a party to the suit and in whose absence an effective decree cannot be passed by the court. Whereas a “proper party” is a person whose presence would enable the court to completely, effectively and properly adjudicate upon all the matters and issues, though he may not be a person in favour of or against whom a decree is to be made. As regards the ‘necessary party’, neither any relief has been prayed against IEX, nor is it the case that no effective order can be passed in the present case in the absence of IEX. Hence, IEX cannot be considered a necessary party. Similarly, we are unable to see how the presence of IEX is required for a complete, effective, and proper adjudication of the matter/issue involved in this case, i.e., the relaxation of the provisions of the PMR 2021 to consider it a proper party.

14. Even in its application, IEX has not made out any case as to how it is a necessary party or, at least, a proper party to the proceedings. All that has been submitted is that the Petitioner, under the guise of Power to Relax, is seeking permission to act contrary to the provision of the PMR 2021, and that too without impleading the other exchanges and affording an opportunity of hearing and representation, particularly when at the stage of the authorisation specific undertaking was given by the Petitioner pursuant to the specific objections being raised. It is

also submitted that IEX has complied with the relevant regulation by having one of its clients surrender its ‘client’ status on its platform within the required timelines under the PMR 2021, and it would be prejudiced if the present Petition is allowed by the Commission. However, these submissions do not in any manner justify IEX being a proper party to this Petition. Whether the Petitioner has made out any case for relaxation of the provisions of the PMR 2021 for grant of time to PTC for diluting its stake to meet the requirement/compliance under Regulation 15 of the PMR 2021 needs to be examined on its own merits. A competing exchange cannot claim an opportunity of a hearing or making representation, as a matter of right, on the ground of being a proper party to such proceedings. Also, the prejudice averred by IEX does not appear to be a prejudice against any direct or legal interest but merely a commercial interest. In view of the above, we find that IEX is neither a necessary nor a proper party to these proceedings and its application for impleadment is therefore liable to be rejected.

The expression “real controversy” refers to the dispute which forms the subject matter of the proceedings as originally instituted. Amendments are ordinarily permitted where they clarify existing pleadings, bring on record subsequent developments closely connected with the original cause of action, or assist the adjudicatory body in effectively determining the issues already arising in the proceedings. _(e) The Petition is barred by the contract between the parties itself, as also the Doctrine of Past Practice:_ On 11.1.2017, when the Joint Reconciliation Statements were signed, all the payments made by the Respondent were adjusted firstly towards principal amount and thereafter towards LPSC. The Joint Reconciliation Statement is itself a contract between the parties. As such, the appropriation of dues has to be done in accordance with the terms and conditions mutually agreed between the parties under the PPA, read with the contract between the parties in the form of the Joint Reconciliation Statement executed between them. In the present case, DVC and Respondent have specifically agreed to the Joint Reconciliation Statement, which is itself a contract between the parties. The Hon’ble Supreme Court, in a catena of judgments, has held that the conduct of the parties is a relevant factor in the construction of contracts. 8. The Petitioner has filed Written Submissions dated 12.7.2025 on the question of arbitrability of the disputes and has mainly submitted the following:

l. Objections relating to lack of jurisdiction and arbitrability can be raised at any stage of the proceedings, including collateral proceedings, and are required to be examined at the threshold.

9. PSPCL, in its response dated 14.8.2025 filed to the Written Submissions filed by the Petitioner dated 12.7.2025 on the question of arbitrability of the disputes, has mainly submitted the following:

a. The Petitioner had itself, during the hearings held on 21.1.2025 and 25.3.2025, requested that the present matter be taken up after the decision in batch matters concerning arbitrability of tariff and non-tariff disputes, and subsequently sought time on 13.5.2025 to file Written Submissions on arbitrability, which indicates that the issue is not settled in the manner sought to be projected by the Petitioner.

b. The reliance placed by the Petitioner on the judgment of MPPMCL v. DVC and the affirmation thereof by the DVC Supreme Court Order is misplaced and requires proper appreciation in the context of the facts and issues involved in the present case. The said judgment deals with the issue of arbitrability in the context of disputes relating to termination of PPA and the applicability of Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, in proceedings under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act, and lays down the distinction between tariff and non-tariff disputes.

e. The contention of the Petitioner that disputes relating to fixed charges can be treated as non-tariff disputes is erroneous, as fixed charges are inseparable from tariff and cannot be viewed in isolation as purely contractual claims. The comparison sought to be drawn by the Petitioner between the present case and the DVC APTEL case is incorrect and misleading, inasmuch as the primary issue in the DVC APTEL case pertained to the termination of the PPA, whereas the present case concerns the payment of fixed charges forming part of the tariff.

10. We have examined the rival contentions. Petitioner’s contention is that the dispute is contractual in nature and it constitutes a non-tariff dispute; on the contrary, PSPCL’s contention is that the present dispute is a tariff dispute and has to be adjudicated by the Commission. Thus, the limited issue before us at this stage is whether the dispute raised by the Petitioner in the present Petition constitutes a tariffrelated dispute or a non-tariff dispute and whether the same falls under the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act?

## 18. Clause 6 of the PPA provides for a dispute resolution mechanism, and it is as

_The power conferred on the Central Commission to adjudicate disputes is confined only to those disputes involving (1) generating companies or (2) transmission licensees. As long as the dispute involves a generating company or a transmission licensee, and even if the other parties to the dispute are neither generating companies nor transmission licensees, the Central Commission would have jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes._

30. In view of the above, since the issue raised in the present proceedings relates to fixed/ capacity charges, which constitute a component of the tariff, it falls within the regulatory domain of the tariff. We take note of the submission of the Petitioner that disputes arising out of alleged contractual breaches under the PPA, which do not impact tariff determination or regulation, fall outside the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission, while relying on the judgment of the APTEL in MPPMCL v. DVC. However, in light of the subsequent judgment in the Mundra UMPP batch, the earlier reliance placed on the judgment dated 28.8.2024 in MPPMCL v. DVC no longer advances the case of the Petitioner. The law now stands clarified that disputes relating to the regulatory functions of the Commission, or which impact tariff either directly or indirectly, are non-arbitrable, notwithstanding an arbitration agreement. It is also observed that though the Petitioner has characterised the dispute as arising from nonscheduling of power and consequent contractual breach, the nature of the relief sought is determinative. Even though non-scheduling may arise from contractual conduct, the consequence sought, namely the recovery of fixed/capacity charges, is governed by tariff principles and forms an integral part of the tariff framework regulated by the Commission.

32. In view of the foregoing analysis, the Commission holds that the present Petition raises a tariff-related dispute falling squarely within the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act. The Commission is empowered and duty-bound to adjudicate the dispute on the merits and is not required to refer it to arbitration.

During the pendency of the appeal, MOP/CEA felt the need to bring greater clarity to the SOP dated 10.03.2023 and to simplify and further streamline it . CEA issued the revised SOP dated 14.01.2025.

- (f)   The SOP dated 14.01.2025 empowers the Regional Power Committee (“RPC”) to grant _deemed_ availability in cases where ISTS transmission lines are affected due to road construction or infrastructure works undertaken by Project Developers such as the BRO. Considering the same Hon’ble Tribunal granted liberty for availing any such remedies as are available to them in law, insofar as the proceedings dated 14.01.2025 are concerned. In view of the liberty granted by the Hon’ble Tribunal, and in light of the SOP dated 14.01.2025, Petitioner submitted a representation to the NRPC on 13.02.2025 to review the availability granted for the period January - February 2022 while _inter alia_ stating that the excavation work undertaken by the BRO within the right of way of Petitioner destabilized its tower at location 286 (“Impacted Tower”) leading to the alteration of SA Line section.

- (v) Hence, the case of the Petitioner, in essence and spirit, is covered by the aforementioned SOP.

- (o) Petitioner was compelled to undertake the shutdown due to safety-critical exigencies caused by third-party activities, over which it had no control. This aspect has subsequently also been factored into the SOP dated 14.01.2025 by MOP/CEA. Petitioner is largely within the scope of SOP dated 14.01.2025, and the NRPC ought to have granted necessary relief.

**6.** Petitioner’s rejoinder dated 26.09.2025 sets out the following submissions:

- d) Petitioner is not joining issues with BRO, as that dispute is already pending before the Hon’ble Tribunal. The present Petition is confined solely to relief under Clause 14 of the revised SOP dated 14.01.2025, which expressly provides that past outages arising from infrastructure works of agencies such as BRO, NHAI, and Railways be treated as deemed available.

**7.** During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for Petitioner put forth the facts of the case. After hearing the parties, the Commission reserved the matter for Order with liberty to the parties to file their respective written submissions, if any.

**8.** Petitioner vide its written submissions dated 29.11.2025 has mainly submitted its earlier arguments.  Additionally, Petitioner has submitted as under:

- (a) Petition No. 318/MP/2022, could not examine the substantive entitlement of the Petitioner, as the then existing SOP dated 10.03.2023 was prospective and excluded the SA Line outage of January–February 2022. Hence, the earlier decision was not a pronouncement on rights but a consequence of the absence of enabling law.

The relevant extract of said Order is as under:

**14.** We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and Respondents and perused the information available on record. Petitioner is praying that the ‘Revised Standard

**15.** The Relevant extracts of the Order dated 19.04.2024 in Petition No. 318/MP/2022 are as below:

_29 (v).  NRPC vide letter dated 14.02.2023 clarified the reasons for not considering the request of the petitioner for deemed availability. The relevant extracts are as under:_

_In view of the above discussions, all the prayers of the Petitioner are rejected.”_

**16.** The Petitioner has submitted that it does not seek the reopening of technical or factual findings recorded earlier in Order 19.04.2024 in Petition No. 318/MP/2022, which are presently under challenge before the Appellate Tribunal. The prayers of the Petitioner are limited to whether the deemed availability for the period 20.01.2022 to 08.02.2022 is required to be examined and granted afresh in terms of the CEA Revised Standard Operating Procedure dated 14.01.2025 by the NRPC.

**25.** Even if it is presumed that the revised SOP is applicable to the Petitioner’s case for the period January-February 2022, such an assumption would lead to ambiguity, in a manner that SOPs have an overriding effect on the OM dated 03.08.2022. The SOP dated 10.02.2023, as it records that deemed availability cases for past shifting of lines, where the diversion work has already been completed, shall not be considered, would mean that the cases between 03.08.2022 and 10.02.2023 shall also not get covered under this SOP, rejecting MOP OM stipulations. Accordingly, MOP OM is the cut-off date for considering or rejecting deemed availability cases. As earlier SOP dated 10.02.2023 has been replaced by the revised SOP, not the MOP OM dated 03.08.2022. Accordingly, the revised SOP, as per the presumption, would be lenient to accept cases up to the date of MOP OM dated 03.08.2022.

**29.** We are of the opinion that the Petition lacks sufficient grounds to be admitted; accordingly, the Petition as well as the prayers of the Petitioner stand rejected.

(b) The contentions of the Petitioner in the present Petition, which are contrary to/in the teeth of the findings rendered by this Commission in the order dated 30.12.2019, read with the order dated 6.12.2021, can never be termed as a “dispute” under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003. Once an issue has been decided by this Commission, any party seeking to act in a manner contrary to/in violation of the judgment can never contend that such conduct is a “dispute”, for seeking to invoke the jurisdiction of the Commission u/s 79(1)(f) of the 2003 Act. There is no “dispute” permitting the Petitioner to file the present Petition, which deserves to be rejected, at the threshold itself, on this ground as well.

(g) From a bare perusal of the literal meaning of ‘dispute’, which means disagreement between the parties, the present issue squarely falls under the definition of dispute as provided under section 79 (1)(f) of the Act, and therefore, is triable by this Commission. Without prejudice to the above submissions, it is submitted that Order 7 Rule 11of the CPC lays down the guiding principles for rejection of any plaint or dismissal of any suit on maintainability. It is evident that there does not exist any ground for seeking rejection of the present Petition. Further, KSEBL and TANGEDCO have failed to establish any of the above conditions, which go to the root of the present matter and warrant its dismissal on maintainability itself. Therefore, in terms of above, it is evident that the present petition is maintainable, as the plain reading of the averment made in the Petition, would evince that there arises a cause of action, as soon as KSEBL has refused to honour the invoices dated 6.1.2022 raised in terms of Regulation 8(6) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations, and continues to subsist as same remains unpaid by KSEBL. Thus, the main thrust of KSEBL that there does not exist a cause of action to initiate the present proceedings as the same is barred by the principle of res judicata, is not based on the correct position of law and cannot be sustained.

(h) The contentions raised by KSEBL are factual in nature, which requires a detailed hearing, and therefore the present Petition is liable to be heard on merits, as the action of non-honouring the invoices raised by the Petitioner, and re-agitating the same issue again and again to prolong the legitimate claim of the Petitioner, is unknown to settled judicial principles. It is a settled position of law that while considering whether the present Petition is maintainable or not, this Commission can only examine whether the present Petition _prima facie_ shows a cause of action, and there cannot be embarkment upon the veracity of the averments made in the Petition (Reliance placed on _D. _No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court._

and substantially similar, the question of issue estoppel does not arise. ## **CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION NEW DELHI** 

## **Petition No. 02/SM/2026 (Suo-Motu)** 

**Coram:  Shri Jishnu Barua, Chairperson Shri Ramesh Babu. V, Member Shri Harish Dudani, Member Shri. Ravinder Singh Dhillon, Member Date of Order:  30[th] March, 2026** 

## **IN THE MATTER OF** 

Directions for removal of difficulty in implementation of the provision in Regulation 9(7) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Deviation Settlement Mechanism and Related Matters) Regulations, 2024. 

## **ORDER** 

The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Deviation Settlement Mechanism and Related Matters) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “DSM Regulations, 2024”/ “Principal Regulation”) were notified on 05.08.2024 and came into effect from 16.09.2024 except for Regulation 8 (8) of the DSM Regulations, 2024. Subsequently, the Commission notified the DSM (1st Amendment) Regulations, 2024 on 17.12.2024, whereby Regulation 3 and Regulation 8(8) of the Principal Regulations were amended with effect from 23.12.2024. Thereafter, the Commission notified the DSM (2[nd] Amendment), 2025 on 25.06.2025, whereby Regulation 8(8) of the Principal Regulations was further amended with effect from 01.07.2025. 

2. Regulation 9(7) of the Principal Regulations provides for the settlement of a deficit in the Deviation and Ancillary Service (DAS) Pool Account. In terms of the said provision, for the period beyond 01.04.2026, any deficit in the DAS Pool Account is to be shared in the ratio of the shortfall of reserves allocated by the National Load Despatch Centre (NLDC) to such Designated ISTS Consumers (DICs). The said provision also stipulates that NLDC shall prepare a detailed procedure for the recovery of charges in the event of a deficit in the DAS Pool Account, including the methodology for computing the shortfall of reserves 

and allocating the deficit amongst DICs. 

3. The extract of Regulation 9(7) of the DSM Regulations, 2024 is as follows: 

_“(7) In case of deficit in the Deviation and Ancillary Service Pool Account of a region, the surplus amount available in the Deviation and Ancillary Service Pool Accounts of other regions shall be used for settlement of payment under clause (6) of this Regulation: Provided that in case the surplus amount in the Deviation and Ancillary Service Pool Accounts of all other regions is not sufficient to meet such deficit, the balance amount shall be recovered from the drawee DICs -  (i) for the period from the date of effect of these regulations till 31.03.2026, in the ratio of [50% in proportion to their drawal at the ISTS periphery] and [50% in proportion to their GNA]; and (ii) from 01.04.2026, in the ratio of the shortfall of reserves allocated by NLDC to such DICs: Provided further that the NLDC shall prepare, with the approval of the Commission, a detailed procedure for recovery of charges in case of deficit in the Deviation and Ancillary Service Pool Accounts, and for the methodology of computation of shortfall of reserves and allocation of deficit amongst DICs._ 

4. In pursuance of the above provisions, the Grid India/ NLDC has reported operational challenges pertaining to high reserve requirement and suggested the need to establish an appropriate methodology for quantification, declaration of reserves by SLDC, measurement of actual reserves, as well as despatch and settlement of reserves mechanism. Accordingly, additional time is considered necessary to establish the requisite framework for the effective implementation of the said provisions. 

5. Therefore, in view of the above implementation issue, the Commission considers it a fit case to exercise the powers conferred under Regulation 12 (Power to Remove Difficulty) of the DSM Regulations, 2024. 

6. Regulation 12 of the DSM Regulations, 2024 provides as follows: 

   - “ _12. Power to Remove Difficulty If any difficulty arises in giving effect to these regulations, the Commission may on its own motion or on an application filed by any affected party, issue such practice directions as may be considered necessary in furtherance of the objective of these regulations.”_ 

7. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred under Regulation 12 of the DSM Regulations, 2024, the Commission issues the following directions: 

   - (i) Sub-clause(i) of Regulation 9(7) of the DSM Regulations, 2024 shall, unless notified otherwise, continue to remain in force till 04.10.2026 (as against 31.03.2026) and sub-clause(ii) of Regulation 9(7) shall, unless notified otherwise, come into effect from 05.10.2026 (as against 01.04.2026) onwards. 

8. Petition No. 02/SM/2026 is disposed of in terms of the above.

6. The instant petition was filed on 21.07.2023. During the hearing held on 22.09.2023, after considering NGEL’s submissions, the Commission admitted the petition and directed the parties to file their replies and rejoinders. During the hearing held on 03.01.2024, the Commission again permitted the Respondents, Telangana Discoms, to file their reply, and NGEL was thereafter permitted to file its rejoinder. On 02.07.2025, on the request of the Respondents, the Commission adjourned the matter to the next date. During the hearing  on 10.09.2025, NGEL submitted that the pleadings were complete and that the issues involved were squarely covered by the previous orders of the Commission. The matter may be reserved for order with both sides permitted to file their written submissions, if any. Whereas, the Respondents, Telangana Discoms, prayed for another opportunity of an oral hearing. Considering the submissions made by the learned counsel for the parties, the Commission adjourned the matter with  a direction to both sides to file their written submissions/ notes of arguments. During the hearing held on 10.11.2025, the contracting parties made detailed submissions and concluded their respective arguments. The matter was reserved for order with the direction to both sides to file the written submissions, if any.

- a) At the outset is submitted that the present petition is misconceived, not maintainable in law and liable to be dismissed _in limine_ .

- d) The notices dated 19.07.2022, 04.11.2022 & 16.11.2022 issued by NGEL informing about the Change in Law events indicated that the said impact, which shall be passthrough in Usage Charges, would be informed separately in due course along with details of expenditure towards BCD and GST and necessary documents. However, to date, no such information has been shared with the Respondents, and in fact, vide the letter dated 16.11.2022, NGEL intimated the Respondents that it was approaching the Commission by filing a petition seeking compensation. In light of the above, the contention of NGEL that Respondents did not respond to any of the notices is vehemently opposed, since NGEL failed to furnish complete details along with supporting documents for verification by the DISCOMs, and also the corresponding change/ revision in usage charges in view of this Change in Law impact was also not communicated by NTPC/NGEL.

- c) The Respondents lodged no contemporaneous objection with MNRE or SECI at the time when the extensions were granted. The O.M.s of 13.08.2020, 29.06.2021, and 02.06.2021, and the SCoD extensions that followed, remained unchallenged by the Respondents for years and drew power from all these projects. Their present plea that they “ought to have been consulted” is therefore an afterthought, unsupported by any record of protest during the critical period. The Respondents’ belated letter relied upon in their reply cannot override or dilute binding ministerial and nodal-agency decisions taken much earlier.

12. We have heard the learned counsels for NGEL (the Petitioner) and Respondents and have carefully perused the records and considered the submissions of the parties.

18. From the above, we observe that NGEL has already informed the Respondents about the extension of time in SCoD under different circumstances. We observe that the present petition is limited to seeking a declaration of change in law and consequential reliefs. In view of the above, we are of the view that the objections raised by the Respondents are beyond the scope of the instant petition.

_The Commission may, at any stage of the proceedings in a petition, allow either party to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy between the parties:_

As per the above, the Commission may allow either party to alter or amend its pleadings, necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy, in such a manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate _at any stage of proceedings_ in a Petition _._ However, the first _proviso_ stipulates that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the commencement of the final hearing of the Petition, unless the Commission is of the opinion that, in spite of due diligence, the

23. On a careful examination of the IA, it clearly appears that the Petitioner has sought the further amendment to the Petition merely to incorporate its claims of Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, along with the consequential reliefs arising therefrom. Pertinently, the Petition already seeks recognition and declaration of various Force Majeure and Change in Law events that affected the construction of the transmission project and permitting the Petitioner to include the Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, would only allow the effective adjudication of the Petitioner’s claims of Change in Law events that affected the transmission project during the construction phase. Additionally, allowing such an amendment would serve the dominant purpose of avoiding multiplicity of proceedings, as the Petitioner would otherwise be required to file a separate Petition to raise such claims, thereby leading to a fresh round of litigation between the parties over Change in Law events.

26. We have carefully considered the objections raised by the Respondents regarding alleged prejudice, abuse of process, and the delay. The Petitioner has primarily argued that the need for the proposed amendment arose only in view of the change in the regulatory position brought about by the MUML Order. The Petitioner has argued that the Commission, by the said Order, has clarified that no recovery of compensation for Change in Law claims shall commence unless (i) there is express consent from all the beneficiaries of the region, or (ii) the claims have been duly approved by the Commission. As a consequence of this, the Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, for which the Petitioner had earlier reserved its right to file a separate Petition under the Change in Law Rules, are now sought to be incorporated for the adjudication of the Commission in this Petition itself. However, we do not agree with the above submission that the need for the present amendment was triggered by the MUML Order. Noticeably, the position clarified in the MUML Order that the Change in Law Rules do not cover a scenario where the parties are not in agreement with each other as to whether the event constitutes a Change in Law event

29. Similarly, the argument of the Respondents that allowing the amendment will prolong litigation and lead to financial prejudice/ cost escalation of unverified claims is also misplaced. Such prejudice, however, is not caused by the amendment, but by the pendency of the main Petition itself, and can be adequately addressed by granting opportunity to the Respondents to file replies, raise objections, or address the merits at the stage of final adjudication. No irreparable prejudice that cannot be compensated or addressed procedurally has been shown. If the present amendment is refused, the Petitioner would then be required to file a fresh Petition in relation to the events occurring on and after 21.10.2021. This would be contrary to the objective of avoiding multiplicity of litigation. Moreover, as already discussed, the proposed amendment neither seeks to change the Petition’s basic nature nor introduces time-barred claims. In our view, the proposed amendment satisfies the legal tests under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, Regulation 38 of the Conduct of Business Regulations, and the well-established principles governing the Amendment of Pleadings as culled out in _Sanjeev Builders (supra)_ .

# **CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION NEW DELHI** 

## **Diary No. IA. 145/2026** 

**In Diary No. 54/2026** 

## **Coram:** 

**Shri Jishnu Barua, Chairperson Shri Ramesh Babu V., Member Shri Harish Dudani, Member Shri Ravinder Singh Dhillon, Member** 

**Date of Order: 17[th] March, 2026** 

## **In the matter of:** 

Application for waiver of Payment of Court Fee Under Section 79 and Section 94(2) of the Electricity Act, 2003 as read with Regulation 26 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023. 

## **And** 

**In the matter of:** 

## **Bhakra Beas Management Board,** 

SLDC Complex, Industrial Area PH-1, BBMB, Chandigarh-160002.                                                                                 … **Petitioner** 

## **Versus** 

## **1. MACLEC Technical Project Laboratory Private Limited,** A-1/153, Safdarjung Enclave, New Delhi-110029. 

## **2. Punjab State Power Corporation Limited,** 

Haryana Power Purchase Centre The Mall, Patiala - 147001. 

**3. UHBVN, IP 3&4, 4[th] Floor, Sector-14** Panchkula- 134113, Haryana. 

## **4. DHBVNL, Vidyut Sadan,** 

Vidyut Nagar, Hisar -125005, Haryana. 

## **5. Rajasthan Urja Vikas Nigam Limited,** 

Vidyut Bhawan, Janpath, Jaipur – 302005, Rajasthan. 

## **6. Himachal Pradesh State Electricity Board,** 

Vidyut Bhawan, Shimla 171004, Himachal Pradesh. 

Order in Diary No. IA. 145/2026 In Diary No. 54/2026 

Page 1 

**7. Chandigarh Electricity Department,** Superintending Engineer, Electricity “OP” Circle, Room No. 511, 5[th] Floor, UT Secretariat (Deluxe) Building, Sector 9D, U.T., Chandigarh - 160009. 

**…Respondents** 

## **ORDER** 

The Applicant, Bhakra Beas Management Board (hereinafter referred to as **“** BBMB”) has filed the instant Interlocutory Application (hereinafter referred to as the “IA”) seeking waiver of the filing fee of Rs. 25,00,000/- in respect of the Petition (Diary No. 54/2026) for the adoption of discovered through the transparent competitive bidding process. 

2. The Petitioner, Bhakra Beas Management Board (hereinafter referred to as **“** BBMB”), has filed the Petition under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 seeking adoption/approval of tariff for 1 MW Power from surface Hydrokinetic Power Project under Renewable Energy Service Company (‘RESCO’) mode for 40 years, at a tariff of Rs. 3.39/kWh determined through competitive bidding process conducted by BBMB. 

3. The Applicant in the IA has submitted as under: 

(a) BBMB is a statutory body constituted under the provisions of Section 79(1) read with Section 80(6) of the Punjab Re-organisation Act, 1966, on the re-organisation of the erstwhile State of Punjab on 1.11.1966. BBMB has been engaged in regulating the supply of water, generation and transmission of power from the Bhakra Nangal and Beas Projects, and in making the power 

Order in Diary No. IA. 145/2026 In Diary No. 54/2026 

Page 2 

available to the Partner States, namely the States of Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, and the Union Territory of Chandigarh. 

(b) Pursuant to the mandate to explore renewable energy opportunities, BBMB issued the Tender Document on 23.05.2025 for Design, engineering, supply, installation, commissioning, own, operation, and Maintenance for a period of 40 years of 4x250 kWh Surface Hydrokinetic Power Plant at Tail Race Channel of Kotla Hydro Power Station, BBMB under RESCO mode. 

(c) Pursuant to the tender, BBMB issued a Letter of Award to MACLEC as Power Developer on 23.10.2025 for design, engineering, supply, installation, commissioning, own, operation, and maintenance for a period of 40 years of 4X250 kW Surface Hydrokinetic Power Plant at Tail Race Channel of Kotla Hydro Power Station, BBMB under RESCO mode, for supply of power to BBMB at the lowest discovered tariff of Rs. 3.39 per Unit. Accordingly, BBMB has filed the Petition on 29.1.2026 seeking adoption of the tariff discovered through   a transparent competitive bidding process. 

(d) As, the present Petition pertains to the adoption of tariff for a small pilot renewable energy project of only 1 MW capacity, which is proposed to be developed using Surface Hydrokinetic technology, an emerging renewable energy technology. 

(e) Considering the nature of the project and the small capacity involved, the requirement to deposit the filing fee of Rs. 25,00,000/- would be disproportionate to the nature and scale of the project, particularly when the 

Order in Diary No. IA. 145/2026 In Diary No. 54/2026 

Page 3 

Petition merely seeks regulatory adoption of tariff discovered through a transparent competitive bidding process. 

4. In the above facts and circumstances, the Applicant has prayed for the waiver of payment of the court fees. 

5. The IA is being decided by circulation. 

6. We have considered the submissions of the Applicant.  The Applicant has submitted that the requirement to deposit the filing fee of Rs. 25,00,000/- is wholly disproportionate to the nature and scale of the project, particularly given that it is a small-capacity pilot project based on emerging renewable energy technology. Considering the submissions of the Applicant, we find that the instant case is fit for exercising the power to relax to reduce the filing fee for the adoption of tariff. Accordingly, in exercise of the power conferred under Regulation 13 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Payment of Fees) Regulations, 2012, which empowers the Commission to relax any provisions of said Regulations, in appropriate cases, the Commission taking into consideration the nature and scale of the project relaxes the provisions of Regulation 4 of the Payment of Fees Regulations 2012. Accordingly, the Petitioner is directed to deposit a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh Only), as application fee for the adoption of tariff for the 1 MW Surface Hydrokinetic Pilot Power Project. 

7. Further, the observations/findings in this IA are case-specific and shall not be cited as a precedent in any other proceedings. 

Order in Diary No. IA. 145/2026 In Diary No. 54/2026 

Page 4 

8. The Registry is directed to list the main Petition (Diary No. 54/2026) on **25.3.2026** , upon receipt of the filing fee of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rs. One lakh only) from the Petitioner. 

9. IA is disposed of in terms of the above. 

Sd/sd/sd/sd/-

ASEB, TSECL and Electricity Departments of Government of Manipur and Mizoram referring to the provisions of Regulation 4(3) of the Congestion charge regulations have argued that congestion charge should not be applied on upstream entities for underdrawal. Regulation 4(3) of the Congestion charge regulations is extracted as under:_

_“(3) The congestion charge shall be payable by the overdrawing regional entity in addition to the Unscheduled Interchange charges which would be payable as per Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Unscheduled Interchange charges and related Matters) Regulations,2009 or any re-enactment thereof.”_

_6. The purpose of the Regulation 4(3) as quoted above is to ensure that the overdrawing entity is made to pay the UI charges as well as charges for congestion, since in the normal shortage scenario, the frequency is mostly below 50 Hz. and it would mostly be the overdrawing entity on the downstream side which would be at fault. However, this does not preclude the under-drawing entity from payment of congestion charges in case the frequency is above 50 Hz._

_14. The Commission is of the view that penalty for congestion cannot be imposed on a control area, primarily because it is smaller in size, though it may have a greater effect. As stated above, the prevalent frequency would decide which side is responsible for the congestion and congestion charge shall be applied accordingly. It is therefore prudent that the size of the control area does not dictate on whom congestion charge is to be applied._

Act, 1956, has established a 24 MW small hydro power project at Dummaguden Village and Mandal in Khammam District, Telangana, on the left flank of a branch of the Godavari River. The generating station achieved synchronization on 9.12.2013 and was declared under commercial operation on 26.1.2014. The Petitioner has been supplying power through Inter-State Short Term Open Access (STOA) to the Indian Energy Exchange (IEX) through collective transactions via a trading licensee.

Petition under Section 14 of the Electricity Act 2003 read with Regulation 6 of the CERC (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of trading licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2020 for the grant of a Category V Inter-State Trading Licence.

The Petitioner, Greennsure Trading Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Petitioner’), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, read with Regulation 6 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for the Grant of Trading Licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as “the Trading Licence Regulations”), amended from time to time, has filed the present Petition for the grant of a Category ‘V’ trading licence for inter-State trading in electricity in all over India.

2. In accordance with sub-Section (2) of Section 15 of the Act read with Clause (4) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations, notices were published by the Petitioner on 27.12.2025 in the ‘Indian Express’ (Lucknow, Kolkata, Jaipur, Delhi and Chandigarh and throughout all the States in North-eastern region of India editions), in the ‘Financial Express’ (Pune, Mumbai, Lucknow, Kochi, Hyderabad, Delhi, Chennai, Chandigarh, Bengaluru and Pune editions) and in the E-newspaper of Indian Express (Belagavi, Bangaluru, Bhubaneshwar, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dharmapuri, Hubbali, Hyderabad, Kalaburagi, Kuchi, Kozhikode, Maduri, Nagapattinam, Sambalpur, Shivamogga, Thiruvananthapuram, Tiruchy, Tirunelveli, Vellore, Vijayawada, Villupuram, Visakhapatnam).  The Petitioner has submitted that no objections have been received in response to the public notices.

4. On the above consideration, the Commission, vide its order dated 17.2.2026, had proposed to grant a Category 'V' inter-State trading licence to the Petitioner. The relevant portions of the said order dated 17.2.2026 are extracted as under:

_14. On consideration of the above facts, after a preliminary examination, we find that the Petitioner meets the requirements as specified in the Trading Licence Regulations for the grant of a Category 'V' trading licence. In view thereof, the Commission proposes to grant a Category 'V' trading licence to the Petitioner. We direct that a notice under Clause (a) of Sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act be issued inviting further suggestions or objections to the proposal of the Commission.”_

(a) of sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act was published in all editions of the Indian Express (English) and Hindustan (Hindi) on 19.2.2026. No suggestions or objections have been received in response to the Commission’s notice.

6. The case was called out for the hearing on 26.2.2026. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that no objection had been received in response to the public notice published by the Commission under subSection (5) of Section 15 of the Act. He further submitted that the Petitioner’s company would comply with the requirements specified in the Trading Licence Regulations during the subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25 years, if granted.

7.      Clause (9) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as under:

_“(9) On consideration of further objections or suggestions received and the reply of the applicant thereto, if any, the Commission may grant the licence or reject the application, for reasons to be recorded in writing if the application does not confirm to the provisions of the Act, the rules or regulations or provisions of any other law for the time being in force:_

_Provided that no application shall be rejected, unless the applicant has been given an opportunity of being heard.”_

8. On consideration of the materials on record, we are satisfied that the Petitioner

company meets the requirements of the Act and the Trading Licence Regulations for the grant of an inter-State trading licence for a Category 'V'.

9. The grant of the trading licence to the Petitioner (hereinafter referred to as “the licensee”) is subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions throughout the period of subsistence of the licence:

- (a) The licensee shall comply with the provisions of the Act, the Rules, and the Regulations, particularly Trading Licence Regulations, orders, and directions issued by the Commission, from time to time, and any other law in force;

- (b) The licensee shall comply with orders and directions issued by the Commission from time to time;

- (f) The licensee shall continue to be governed by the qualifications and disqualifications specified in Chapter 2 of the Trading Licence Regulations during the subsistence of the licence;

- (g) The licensee shall continue to abide by the terms and conditions of the licence specified in Chapter V of the Trading Licence Regulations, as amended from time to time;

- (i) Non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, Rules, Regulations, and the provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations shall make the licence of the Petitioner liable for revocation;

- (j) If the licensee fails to undertake trading in electricity within a year from the date of the licence, the licence shall be liable for revocation in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Trading Licence Regulations; and

- (k) The licensee shall submit all such reports or information as may be required under Trading Licence Regulations or any other regulations of the Commission or as per the directions of the Commission as may be issued from time to time.

items.subject: Application under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Regulation 6 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of trading license and other related matters), Regulations, 2020 for grant of an inter-state trading licence. items.pdf_digest:
**Parties present:** Shri Aditya K Singh, Advocate, KPEL Shri Vineet Gupta, Advocate, KPEL Shri Divyansh Singh, Advocate, KPEL

The Petitioner, K.P. Energy Limited (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Petitioner’), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, has made the present application under Sections 14 of the Electricity Act, 2013 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) read with Regulation 6(1) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for the Grant of Trading Licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as “the Trading Licence

Regulations”), amended from time to time, has filed the present Petition for the grant of a Category ‘V’ trading licence for inter-State trading in electricity in the whole of India.

2. In accordance with sub-Section (2) of Section 15 of the Act read with Clause (4) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations, notices were published by the Petitioner on 6.12.2025 in the ‘Business Standard’ (Chandigarh, Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Mumbai, Pune, Bangalore, Bhubaneshwar, Chennai, Kochi, Kolkata, Delhi, Lucknow, Guwahati and Bhopal editions) and in “The Financial Express” (Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Chandigarh, Kolkata, Mumbai, Pune, Ahmedabad (including Gujarati language), Delhi and Lucknow editions). The Petitioner has submitted that no objections have been received in response to the public notices.

4. On the above consideration, the Commission, vide its order dated 31.1.2026, had proposed to grant a Category 'V' inter-State trading licence to the Petitioner. The relevant portions of the said order dated 31.1.2026 are extracted as under:

_22. The Memorandum of Association authorises the Petitioner company to engage in the transmission of electricity. The Petitioner, vide its affidavit dated 15.12.2025, has submitted that it will not carry out the transmission business without surrendering the trading licence, if granted by the Commission._

_23. On consideration of the above facts, after a preliminary examination, we find that the Petitioner meets the requirements as specified in the Trading Licence Regulations for the grant of a Category 'V' trading licence. In view thereof, the Commission proposes to grant a Category 'V' trading licence to the Petitioner. We direct that a notice under Clause (a) of Sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act be issued inviting further suggestions or objections to the proposal of the Commission.”_

(a) of sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act was published in all editions of the Hindustan Times (English) and Amar Ujala (Hindi) on 6.2.2026. No suggestions or objections have been received in response to the Commission’s notice.

6. The case was called out for the hearing on 19.2.2026. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that no objection had been received in response to the public notice published by the Commission under sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act. He further submitted that the Petitioner’s company would comply with the requirements specified in the Trading Licence Regulations during the subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25 years, if granted.

7.      Clause (9) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as under:

_“(9) On consideration of further objections or suggestions received and the reply of the applicant thereto, if any, the Commission may grant the licence or reject the application, for reasons to be recorded in writing if the application does not confirm to the provisions of the Act, the rules or regulations or provisions of any other law for the time being in force:_

_Provided that no application shall be rejected, unless the applicant has been given an opportunity of being heard.”_

8. On consideration of the materials on record, we are satisfied that the Petitioner company meets the requirements of the Act and the Trading Licence Regulations for the grant of an inter-State trading licence for a Category 'V'.

9. The grant of the trading licence to the Petitioner (hereinafter referred to as “the licensee”) is subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions throughout the period of subsistence of the licence:

- (a) The licensee shall comply with the provisions of the Act, the Rules, and the Regulations, particularly Trading Licence Regulations, orders, and directions issued by the Commission, from time to time, and any other law in force;

- (b) The licensee shall comply with orders and directions issued by the Commission from time to time;

- (g) The licensee shall continue to abide by the terms and conditions of the licence specified in Chapter V of the Trading Licence Regulations, as amended from time to time;

- (i) Non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, Rules, Regulations, and the provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations shall make the licence of the Petitioner liable for revocation;

- (k) The licensee shall submit all such reports or information as may be required

under Trading Licence Regulations or any other regulations of the Commission or as per the directions of the Commission as may be issued from time to time.

10. An extract of a copy of this order be sent to the Central Government (the Ministry of Power) and the Central Electricity Authority in terms of sub-Section (7) of Section 15 of the Act for their information and record.

The Petitioner, Sikkim Urja Limited (formerly Teesta Urja Limited) (in short ‘SUL’), has filed the present Petition under Sections 142, 146, and 149 of the Electricity Act, 2003 seeking enforcement of the Order dated 22.11.2022 in Petition No. 110/MP/2019 against Respondents No. 1 to 3, namely Haryana Power Purchase Centre (HPPC), Uttar Haryana Bijlee Vitran Nigam Limited and Dakshin Haryana Bijlee Vitran Nigam Limited (collectively referred to as the ‘Haryana Utilities’) on account of their alleged non-compliance in respect of payment of amount due and commencement of scheduling and offtake of the contracted capacity from the generating station of the Petitioner.

   - (a) _“Initiate action under Section 142, 146 and 149 and other applicable provisions of the Electricity Act against the Respondent No. 1 to 3 for willful and wanton violation of the Order dated 22.11.2022 of the Hon’ble Commission in non-payment of the arrears to the Petitioner and scheduling electricity from the Project of the Petitioner;_

   - (c) _Direct Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 to pay difference in tariff determined by this Hon’ble Commission, after adjustment of revenue from sale under short term/ through exchange for the period beyond June 2023, up to the date of payment & commencement of scheduling of power by Respondent Nos. 1 to 3._ 

   - (d) _Direct the Respondents No. 1 to 3 to pay the late payment surcharge/interest as per the provisions of the PPA/PSA for delayed payment of tariff to the Petitioner as claimed under Prayers (b) and (c) above up to the date of release of payment by Respondent Nos. 1 to 3;_

19. **Manikaran** submitted that the option may be provided in a grace period beyond the compliance timeline, whereby the Obligated/ Designated Entity, if availing the Buyout Price route, must submit a Declaration with a reason for exceeding the compliance period and adopting the Buyout Price route.

24. **CESC** , in contrast, submitted that the Original MoP notification does not prescribe any hierarchy or prioritisation among these options. ## **Background** 

2. The Petitioner had entered into a Power Purchase Agreement dated 2.7.2010 (PPA I) with the Respondent, North Eastern Electric Power Corporation Limited (NEEPCO), for the procurement of power from the Tuirial Hydro Electric Project situated in Kolasib district of Mizoram for a period of five years. Upon expiry of the PPA I, the parties executed a fresh Power Purchase Agreement dated 19.4.2023 (PPA II) to continue power supply for a further period of five years. 

3. The present Petition was filed on 27.11.2024, _inter alia_ , challenging Invoice No. NEEPCO/MIZO/2024-25/1500/SHRTFL/01 dated 30.4.2024 raised by the Respondent towards recovery of shortfall in energy charges for the tariff period 201924. The Petitioner has also filed Interlocutory Application No. 98/2024 seeking interim relief in the nature of a stay on the operation of the impugned invoice and restraining the Respondent from taking any coercive action during the pendency of the Petition. 

4. The dispute pertains to the Respondent’s claim for recovery of Rs. 102.07 crore towards shortfall energy charges under Regulations 65 (7) and 65 (8) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024. The Respondent has attributed the shortfall to factors beyond its control, including variations between maximum possible generation based on available inflows and design energy, transmission constraints leading to energy losses, and lower

scheduling vis-à-vis declared capacity. Subsequently, during a reconciliation meeting held on 4.10.2024, the amount was revised to Rs. 101.21 crore. 

5. The Petition was admitted on 28.11.2024, and in compliance with the directions of the Commission, the Petitioner commenced payment of instalments as per the impugned invoice. Subsequently, the matter was listed for hearing on 26.12.2024, 28.1.2025, 25.3.2025, 8.7.2025, 26.9.2025, 10.11.2025, and 2.1.2026, during which the Commission directed the Petitioner to liquidate the balance of the monthly tariff instalment payment within the stipulated trigger dates. 

## **Hearing dated 10.2.2026** 

6. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that all fifteen instalments under the impugned invoices have been paid to the Respondent, which was duly acknowledged by the learned counsel for the Respondent. In light of these developments, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the reliefs sought in the present Petition no longer survive and, accordingly, sought permission to withdraw the Petition. The learned counsel for the Respondent did not object to the said request. 

7. In view of the above submissions, the present Petition is disposed of as ‘withdrawn’.

_"47. In other words, whether the RoW issue, in particular case, qualifies as a force majeure event or not has to be examined on the basis of the facts & circumstances involved in each case and also the efforts & remedies availed by the licensee to resolve such issues in such case. As already noted above, the Petitioner has submitted the details of correspondences exchanged with various Authorities along with supporting documents. Insofar as they relate to the obstruction/ resistance from the land owners, request for intervention/ assistance of the Govt. Authorities in dealing with them etc. cannot be considered as force majeure event and no relief under force majeure can flow to the Petitioner as such activities are required to be anticipated by the licensee during the course of implementing the projects. However, what have to be distinguished from these generic efforts of resolving the RoW issues are the delays - owing to the stays/ injunctions granted by the Courts and the Court proceedings arising out these RoW issues & in the course of the Petitioner having availed the legal remedies in resolving the RoW issues. 5. The matter was heard on 27.11.2025. After hearing the parties, the matter was reserved for order.

6. The instant Review Petition has been filed under Section 94(1) of the Act read with Section 114 and Order 47 Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as ‘CPC’) and Regulation 52 (2) (B) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023 (hereinafter referred to as “CBR, 2023”) seeking review of the order dated 19.6.2025 passed by the Commission in Petition No. 87/AT/2025.  Regulation 52(2) of the CBR, 2023 provides that an aggrieved party can seek review of a direction, decision or order of the Commission, which is akin to the grounds provided in Order 47 Rule 1 of the CPC. The Review

Petitioner has submitted that at paragraphs 31 & 32 of the impugned Order, the Commission only adopted the tariff for allocated capacity to the respective bidders but not the capacity allocated under the Greenshoe Option to such bidders despite having acknowledged the same.

_“(1) The Commission shall exercise jurisdiction to review its own orders, decisions, and directions in accordance with Clause (f) of sub-section (1) of Section 94 of the Act read with Section 114 and Order 47 of the Civil Procedure Code._

_(2) Any person aggrieved by a direction, decision, or order of the Commission, from which no appeal has been preferred, may file a review petition on the 34 following grounds within forty days of the making of such decision, direction, or order:_

_(a) Upon the discovery of new and important matter or evidence that, after the exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced by him at the time when the direction, decision, or order was passed or;_

9. It is noted that the Review Petitioner had filed Petition No. 87/AT/2025 along

“(a) _Admit the present Petition. (b) Adopt the_ _**Tariff discovered in the Competitive Bidding Process for individual Power Projects as listed in Table-1 at paragraph 9** above on terms and conditions contained in the PPA to be signed with RE-Power Generators being Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 and a Trading Margin of Rs. 0.07 / kWh in addition to above Tariff is to be recovered from buying Utilities /Distribution Licensee/DISCOM(s) in terms of the PSA to be signed between NHPC & Utilities/ Distribution Licensee._

_(c ) Pass such other and further order / orders as are deemed fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case._ ”

12. Therefore, the Review Petitioner has failed to incorporate any specific prayer seeking the relief now claimed in the Review Petition. It is a cornerstone of procedural jurisprudence that no court or tribunal possesses the inherent power to grant a relief not expressly pleaded or prayed for, as this would deny counter-parties a fair opportunity to address the claim and imperil the adversarial process. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of _Bharat Amratlal Kothari v. Dosukhan Samadkhan Sindhi [(AIR 2010 SC 475)]_ has held that a tribunal cannot grant relief not prayed for, disregarding established norms governing the grant of relief.

13. It is apposite to note that the power of the Commission to review its order is concededly restricted and can be exercised only in certain specific circumstances and is limited to errors that are self-evident, without requiring elaborate arguments or interpretation. The Review Petitioner has invoked the provisions of Section 94(1)(f) of the Act and Regulation 52 of the CBR, 2023, on the ground of an ‘error apparent on

the face of the record’ in the impugned order for failing to adopt the tariff pertaining to the ‘Greenshoe option’ quantum. However, as seen above, the order passed by the Commission was confined to the prayers specifically sought by NHPC during the hearing of Petition No. 87/AT/2025. No such patent error has been demonstrated by the Review Petitioner.

14. For the reasons aforementioned, we find no merit in the submissions advanced by the Review Petitioner so as to warrant the entertainment of the present Review Petition. The Review Petition does not disclose any error apparent on the face of the record that merits exercise of review jurisdiction under Section 94(1)(f) of the Act read with Regulation 52 of the CBR, 2023. Accordingly, the Review Petition is rejected. However, considering the important nature of the matter which pertains to green power, the Petitioner is granted liberty to file a fresh Petition specifically seeking adoption of the ‘Greenshoe Option’ quantum, and the same shall be considered in accordance with law.

22. We note that it is a well-settled principle of law that the parties, by their agreement, can neither confer jurisdiction upon a forum that does not have the jurisdiction under the law nor can the parties, by their agreement, oust the jurisdiction of the forum vested under the law.

- _“….where the parties to a contract agreed to submit the disputes arising from it to a particular jurisdiction which would otherwise also be a proper jurisdiction under the law their agreement to the extent they agreed not to submit to other jurisdictions cannot be said to be void as against public policy. If on the other hand the jurisdiction they agreed to submit to would not otherwise be proper jurisdiction to decide disputes arising out of the contract it must be declared void being against public policy.”_

_“By a long series of decisions it has been held that where two Courts or more have under the CPC jurisdiction to try a suit or proceeding an agreement between the parties that the dispute between them shall be tried in any one of such Courts is not contrary to public policy and in no way contravenes Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Therefore, if on the facts of a given case more than one Court has jurisdiction, parties by their consent may limit the jurisdiction to one of the two Courts. But by an agreement parties cannot confer jurisdiction to a Court which otherwise does not have jurisdiction to deal with a matter.”_

25. In the light of the above position of law, we are of the view that merely because the PPA mentions adjudication of the dispute in a specific manner, it cannot oust the jurisdiction of this Commission, which flows from the provisions of the Act. Hence, we hold that adjudication involving the parties will be governed by this Commission under Section 79 (1)(f), read with Section 79(1)(a) of the Act. However, we would like to observe that the Petitioner should have exercised prudence before executing the PPA with KSEBL. The Petitioner was well aware about the applicability of Section 79(1)(a) of the Electricity Act, 2003 which confers jurisdiction upon CERC to regulate the generating companies owned/controlled by the Central Government and should have raised this issue of jurisdiction at the RfS stage itself and more so at the time of signing the PPA, which it did not do so, leading to avoidable confusion about the jurisdiction. We expect the Petitioner to be more responsible in the future and  to make its position clear at the outset when it participates in such state-specific bids. Accordingly, we hold that the matter is covered within the jurisdiction of the Central Commission as per Section 79(1)(a) read with Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003.
